\label{ch:ar-letters-from-please-and-sorry}
\hlchaptermodality{48}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write dad, alif madda, zay and ghayn, and find each one in a word I already say.}

\section[ḍād]{\ar{ض} (ḍād) — the letter inside \ar{فضلك}}

\label{lesson:AR-W48-dad}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ar{ف} and \ar{ق} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}} (\emph{min faḍlik}), \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ar{ض}}
\textbf{\ar{ض}} — \emph{ḍād}, a heavy \emph{d}.

It is inside \textbf{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}} (\emph{min faḍlik}), \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{}. It is \textbf{\ar{ص}} (\emph{ṣād}), which you already write, with \textbf{one dot above}. Arabic is sometimes called \emph{the language of the ḍād}, because the sound is so rare in other languages.

\subsection*{Writing: \ar{ض}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/AR-W48-dad-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ar{ض} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: close the oval clockwise from its lower-left junction
  \item \textbf{2.} turn left and rise into the short shoulder without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} lift, restart at the baseline junction, and sweep through the trailing bowl
  \item \textbf{4.} lift again, then place the upper dot last — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Introduction to Arabic: Egyptian Arabic for first-year students, Alphabet: \ar{س} \ar{ش} \ar{ص} \ar{ض}, independent Daad at 00:43.1–00:46.3 (University of Oregon Libraries Open Textbook, 2023).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}} and point at \ar{ض} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ar{ض} three times, saying \emph{ḍ} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ar{ق}, then \ar{ض}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ar{ض}? (\textbf{ḍād}, \emph{ḍ}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}}, \emph{min faḍlik}, \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[alif madda]{\ar{آ} (alif madda) — the alif that opens \ar{آسف}}

\label{lesson:AR-W48-alif-madda}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ar{ق} and \ar{ض} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ar{آسف}} (\emph{āsif}), \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ar{آ}}
\textbf{\ar{آ}} — \emph{alif} with a \textbf{madda}, a long \emph{ā} at the start of a word.

It opens \textbf{\ar{آسف}} (\emph{āsif}), \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{}. The wavy stroke on top, the \emph{madda}, stretches the vowel: where a plain \textbf{\ar{ا}} at the start of a word needs a hamza to say \emph{a}, \textbf{\ar{آ}} says a long \emph{ā}.

\subsection*{Writing: \ar{آ}}
Put your pen on \ar{آ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start this character or which way to travel}. It is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ar{آسف}} and point at \ar{آ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ar{آ} three times, saying \emph{ā} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ar{ض}, then \ar{آ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ar{آسف}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ar{آ}? (\textbf{alif madda}, \emph{ā}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ar{آسف}}, \emph{āsif}, \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zāy]{\ar{ز} (zāy) — the letter inside \ar{أزرق}}

\label{lesson:AR-W48-zay}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ar{ض} and \ar{آ} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ar{أزرق}} (\emph{azraq}), \textquotedblleft{}blue\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ar{ز}}
\textbf{\ar{ز}} — \emph{zāy}, the sound \emph{z}.

It is inside \textbf{\ar{أزرق}} (\emph{azraq}), \textquotedblleft{}blue\textquotedblright{}, from \textbf{\ar{أحمر} \ar{أزرق}}. It is \textbf{\ar{ر}} (\emph{rāʾ}), which you already write, with \textbf{one dot above}, and like \textbf{\ar{ر}} it never joins to the letter after it.

\subsection*{Writing: \ar{ز}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/AR-W48-zay-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ar{ز} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: begin at the upper tip and descend through the short stroke
  \item \textbf{2.} without lifting, sweep left through the lower curve without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} lift once, then place the dot above — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Introduction to Arabic: Egyptian Arabic for first-year students, Alphabet \ar{ر} \ar{ز} \ar{و}, independent Zay body followed by its upper dot (University of Oregon Libraries Open Textbook, 2023; accessed 2026-08-23).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ar{أزرق}} and point at \ar{ز} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ar{ز} three times, saying \emph{z} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ar{آ}, then \ar{ز}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ar{أزرق}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ar{ز}? (\textbf{zāy}, \emph{z}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ar{أزرق}}, \emph{azraq}, \textquotedblleft{}blue\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ghayn]{\ar{غ} (ghayn) — the letter inside \ar{الغد}}

\label{lesson:AR-W48-ghayn}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ar{آ} and \ar{ز} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ar{إلى} \ar{الغد}} (\emph{ilā l-ghad}), \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ar{غ}}
\textbf{\ar{غ}} — \emph{ghayn}, a \emph{gh} gargled at the back of the throat.

It is inside \textbf{\ar{إلى} \ar{الغد}} (\emph{ilā l-ghad}), \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}. It is \textbf{\ar{ع}} (\emph{ʿayn}), which you already write, with \textbf{one dot above}, the third family where a single dot turns one sound into another.

\subsection*{Writing: \ar{غ}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/AR-W48-ghayn-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ar{غ} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: sweep left from the upper-right tip and shape the open head
  \item \textbf{2.} continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} lift once, then place the upper dot last — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Introduction to Arabic: Egyptian Arabic for first-year students, Alphabet \ar{ع} \ar{غ}, independent Ghayn at 00:02.4–00:04.0 (University of Oregon Libraries Open Textbook, 2023; accessed 2026-08-23).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ar{إلى} \ar{الغد}} and point at \ar{غ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ar{غ} three times, saying \emph{gh} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ar{ز}, then \ar{غ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ar{إلى} \ar{الغد}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ar{غ}? (\textbf{ghayn}, \emph{gh}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ar{إلى} \ar{الغد}}, \emph{ilā l-ghad}, \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
